You write: In 2009, NASA launched the Kepler Space telescope to search for more Earth-sized planets in the Milky Way galaxy. It was designed to look for exoplanets using the transit method, searching for the slight dimming of a star when a planet passes in front of it. This mission is how scientists found the first confirmed planetary system with more than one planet orbiting the same star, which they called Kepler-9. Before this, humans didn’t know of a single planet outside of our solar system, so the discovery of “planets everywhere” basically created an entire new way to explore and understand our galaxy. While it was originally positioned to stare continuously at 150,000 stars in the patch of sky in the Cygnus constellation, it was so successful that scientists decided to extend its mission and shift its point of view about every 3 months. This new leg of the mission was called K2, and used the pressure of sunlight to maintain its pointing after the original mechanism malfunctioned in 2013. Before being retired in 2018, it identified over 2,600 confirmed exoplanets in our galaxy, data which was made available to the public and has led and will continue to lead to many more scientific discoveries.
AI writes: The Kepler Space Telescope was a NASA mission that revolutionized our understanding of planetary systems beyond our own. Launched in 2009 and named after the 17th-century astronomer Johannes Kepler, the spacecraft was designed to search for Earth-sized exoplanets orbiting distant stars within their habitable zones. Using the transit method—detecting the slight dimming of a star's light as a planet passes in front of it—Kepler observed over 150,000 stars during its nearly decade-long mission. The mission was extraordinarily successful, discovering more than 2,600 confirmed exoplanets and fundamentally transforming our knowledge of planetary diversity in the universe. After running out of fuel, Kepler was retired in 2018, but its legacy continues as scientists analyze the vast dataset it collected and as it paved the way for future exoplanet-hunting missions like the James Webb Space Telescope.
